title: Eviction can turn a housing event into residential, school, and educational disruption for children
source_unit: U.S. Census Bureau Center for Economic Studies Working Paper CES 25-34 / NBER Working Paper 33659 linking eviction court, public school, homelessness-service, and restricted Census records in Chicago and New York
geography: Cook County/Chicago and New York City; eviction court cases from roughly 2000–2019 in Cook County and 2007–2017 in New York, with linked school and administrative outcomes

observations.period: Eviction court records and linked child outcomes

denominator.unit: baseline eviction cases before linked-data sample restrictions across Cook County and New York

linked_school_matches.value: 77,256 unique student-case matches in Chicago and 278,879 in New York

data_domains.value: eviction court, public school, homelessness-service, and restricted Census records

identification.value: random assignment of court cases to judges with different eviction leniency

observations.method: Research paper linking administrative records and using judge assignment as an instrument to separate eviction effects from correlated economic distress; Census CES paper has not undergone the review accorded to Census Bureau publications.
observations.uncertainty: The causal design identifies effects for cases marginal to judge assignment and the linked populations in two cities; it is not a national eviction estimate or a universal effect for every child.
observations.subgroup: Children in public school records connected to households in eviction court in Chicago and New York; effects may differ by age, sex, city, family support, and housing context.
observations.counterinterpretation: Judge-assignment estimates apply to cases influenced by judicial leniency, and other eviction, court, school, or family-support contexts may produce different effects.

observations.period: Case year and two academic years after eviction order

denominator.unit: children in the linked instrumental-variable analysis; study-specific denominator varies by outcome and city

residential_mobility.value: +13 percentage points in the case year, approximately doubling the nonevicted mean; effects persisted through the next two academic years

homelessness.value: +7.0 percentage points in Cook County and +3.1 percentage points in New York in the year after filing; effects grew in the following year

test_scores.value: little impact on elementary and middle school test scores

observations.method: Instrumental-variable estimates based on quasi-random judge assignment, with outcomes followed through linked education and homelessness-service records.
observations.uncertainty: Homelessness estimates and longer-run outcomes vary by city, outcome, and available linkage; estimates should not be read as effects of every eviction filing or informal displacement.
observations.subgroup: Children whose households received an eviction order and comparable children in eviction court whose cases were assigned to less-likely-to-evict judges.
observations.counterinterpretation: The result does not show that every child experienced homelessness or school disruption; family support, informal moves, shelter access, and unobserved coping can moderate effects.

observations.period: Descriptive exposure and longer-run education outcomes

denominator.unit: children and households in the linked Chicago/New York court-school records; descriptive compositions and causal estimates use different universes

cases_with_children.unit: share of Cook County eviction cases involving households with children

single_mother_households.unit: share of children facing eviction living in a single-mother-headed household

doubled_up_before_eviction.unit: share of children facing eviction already living in a doubled-up household

high_school_completion.value: eviction reduces high-school graduation; bounding analysis indicates the result is not driven by differential attrition

observations.method: Linked administrative description plus instrumental-variable analysis and a bounding procedure for differential attrition.
observations.uncertainty: Descriptive household composition is not itself causal; high-school completion estimates reflect the study's linked population and method, not all children exposed to eviction nationwide.
observations.subgroup: Children in the Chicago and New York study populations, with effects reported as worse for older children and boys and potentially moderated by family support networks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Eviction is one disruption among broader poverty, health, employment, and housing-market pressures; the design improves causal attribution but does not identify every mechanism or policy remedy.

related_sources.claim: NBER Working Paper 33659 is the associated research-paper version of the eviction-effects study.
Related Census CES work describes linked eviction and student records for parenting and non-parenting college students.

boundary: This record adds a causal housing-to-child-outcome route in two urban settings: eviction order to movement, homelessness, school engagement, and educational outcomes. It does not establish a national eviction effect, the effect of informal displacement, household-level policy receipt, long-term adult outcomes, or which intervention prevents the harm.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Census CES working-paper PDF used for the extracted findings; the paper is an author working paper and the restricted linked data are not locally reproduced.
